The bridge contest in Mr. Okafor's science class had one rule that mattered: a bridge could weigh at most eighty grams, and the one that held the most sand before it broke would win. Dev had spent three weekends on his. It was built of craft sticks and white glue, and he had doubled every triangle, because the library book said triangles were what kept a bridge standing.

On the morning of the test he carried it to school in a shoebox on his lap, with both hands over the lid every time the bus hit a bump.

Mr. Okafor set each bridge across two desks and hung a bucket from its middle. Then he poured in sand from a measuring cup, one cup at a time, while the class counted. Priya's bridge held eleven cups. Marcus's held six and folded with a sound like a cracker. When it was Dev's turn, he lifted the lid of the shoebox and saw that one end of the bridge had come loose. The glue at the joint had dried in a thin skin over a gap he must have missed.

"You can test it now," Mr. Okafor said, "or take it home and fix it. Bridges tested on Friday won't count for the contest."

Dev looked at the gap, and then at the bucket. He said he would test it now.

Priya came up beside him holding a binder clip from her pencil case and asked whether it was allowed. Mr. Okafor put the bridge and the clip together on the kitchen scale he kept on his desk. Seventy-nine grams. He said it was allowed.

Dev clamped the loose end. The class counted. At four cups the bridge creaked, at seven the clip began to slide, and at nine the whole end gave way at once and the bucket dropped onto the desk with a soft thump of sand.

Nine cups put him in third place. On the way out, Dev asked Priya why she had helped him when his bridge might have beaten hers.

"I wanted to see what yours would hold," she said. "I've wanted to since you showed us the drawings."

That night Dev took the bridge out of the box and turned it over under the desk lamp. He found the gap, and then two smaller ones near the middle that he had missed as well. He got out a pencil and began a list of what he would do differently, and at the top he wrote: check every joint, then check it again.

My mother leaves at midnight when it snows.
She zips her coat over the clothes she sleeps in,
takes the thermos from the counter,
and the kitchen light stays on.

From my window I can see the county yard,
the orange truck lit up like a lantern,
its blade lowered to the road the way
a heron lowers its beak to the water.

All night she drives the long loop past the reservoir,
up Quarry Hill, down through the shut-eyed town,
pushing the snow aside in a white wave
that curls and settles along the shoulder.

I fall asleep to the scrape of it, far off,
a sound like someone sweeping a porch
in a house I have never visited.

In the morning the bus comes on time.
The roads are black and wet and open,
and the driver says what he always says:
somebody was up early.

Somebody was. She is asleep by then,
her boots by the door, her gloves
drying on the heater, the thermos
in the sink with the spoon still in it.

Nobody at school knows her name.
They know the roads are clear.
I walk on the street she made
and keep my steps inside the tire tracks,

the way you would walk in someone's footprints
to see where they had gone,
to see how far, all night,
they went for you.

My mother learned to ride a bicycle the summer she turned forty-one. She had grown up above her parents' restaurant in a city where the streets were too crowded for children on bikes, and by the age when she might have learned, she was working the register after school.

I was nine that summer, and I had been riding for three years. When she announced at dinner that she was going to learn, my father put down his fork and asked whether she was sure. She said she had been sure for about thirty years.

She bought a used bicycle at a yard sale on Delmont Avenue, blue, with a wire basket and a bell that had rusted silent. My father lowered the seat until she could set both feet flat on the ground. Then, because I was the one in the family who remembered learning most recently, I was put in charge.

I taught her the way my father had taught me. I held the back of the seat and ran beside her down the gravel lane behind our house. It did not work. She was heavier than I was, and every time the bike tipped I went with it, and twice we ended up in the ditch together, laughing so hard that a neighbor came out to see what had happened.

On the fourth evening she asked me to tell her when I let go. I had planned to keep it a secret, the way my father had with me, and I said so. She said she would rather know. So I counted out loud, one, two, three, and on three I opened my hands and stopped running.

She went eleven yards. I know because I paced it afterward. Then she put her feet down, and the bike stopped, and she stood there in the middle of the lane with her back to me.

I thought she was crying, and I ran up to her. She had come out straight from the dinner dishes, and she was writing in the little notebook she kept in her apron pocket for grocery lists. When I asked what she was doing, she showed me. Under "eggs" and "dish soap" she had written: 11 yds.

By August she was riding to the farm stand on Route 9 and back, three miles, with a melon in the basket. She rode slowly and kept to the edge of the road, and at every driveway she rang the rusted bell anyway, though it made no sound at all.

I have taught other people things since then. But I have never again been so certain that I was watching someone collect a debt the world had owed her for a long time.

Every parent of a young reader knows the request. The last page is turned, and the child closes the book and opens it again at the beginning. Many adults find this a little puzzling. There are thousands of books in the library, they think, and the child is spending an evening on one already read.

I used to think so too. Then I spent a year reading aloud to my nephew, who asked for the same book about a lost mitten roughly two hundred times, and I began to pay attention to what he was doing.

On the first reading he wanted to know what happened. By the tenth he knew what happened and wanted to be there before it did. He would put his hand on the page just before the fox appeared, and wait, and then laugh when it did, as though he had arranged it himself. By the fiftieth reading he was correcting me. If I skipped a line, he noticed; if I changed a word, he restored it.

Somewhere past the hundredth, he started asking questions that a first reading could never have produced. Why did the mole go in first? Was the bear being polite, or did it just want to be warm? Those are questions about character and motive, and he could ask them because the plot had stopped needing his attention.

That is what rereading offers that a new book cannot. A first reading spends most of its effort on finding out. A second reading, freed from that work, has attention left over for how the thing is made: the order of events, the choice of a word, the moment a sentence grows shorter as the danger grows closer. Adults understand this about music. They rarely apologize for playing a favorite song again.

None of this means children should read only the books they know. A diet of the familiar is a narrow one, and new books bring new words and new worlds. But the child who reaches for the same book again is usually doing something more interesting than avoiding the effort of a new one. That child is moving in, learning the rooms of a house well enough to find the way around it in the dark, which is one of the better things a reader can do with a book.

In late spring, a crowded honeybee colony does something that looks at first like a disaster. More than half of its workers, along with the old queen, pour out of the hive in a roaring cloud and gather in a dense cluster on a nearby branch. They leave behind their honey, their wax, and a new queen about to hatch. The cluster hanging from the branch has no home and only a few days of food carried in the bees' stomachs.

What happens next is a kind of election. A few hundred of the oldest bees, the colony's scouts, fly off to search the countryside for a hollow that could serve as a nest. A good site is a cavity of roughly forty liters, well above the ground, with a small entrance. A scout that finds a candidate may spend most of an hour inspecting it, walking its inner walls and flying through its dark interior.

Back on the cluster, the scout reports what she found with a dance. The angle of her run on the surface of the swarm tells the others which direction to fly, and the number of times she repeats the dance reflects how good she judged the site to be. A scout that found an excellent hollow may dance a hundred circuits; one that found a cramped crack in a wall may dance ten and stop. Other bees follow the dancers out to inspect the sites for themselves, and if they agree, they return and dance too.

Over a day or two, the best sites gather more and more supporters while weaker ones fade. The decision, however, is made at the site itself. When scouts visiting a cavity find twenty or thirty others there at once, they fly back and begin a high-pitched piping sound that tells the cluster to warm its flight muscles. Within an hour the whole swarm lifts off and flies, guided by the scouts, to its new home.

Researchers who have offered swarms several nest boxes of different quality find that the swarm usually chooses the best one, even though most scouts have visited only one of the choices. The good judgment belongs to the group. It emerges from a simple rule each bee follows: dance in proportion to the quality of what you found, and let your dancing taper off with time.
